claim: Trypanosoma brucei presents an excellent model for studies on codon bias and differential gene expression because transcription is broadly unregulated and uniform across the genome.
source: Trypanosoma brucei presents an excellent model for studies on codon bias and differential gene expression because transcription is broadly unregulated and uniform across the genome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T. brucei's transcriptional characteristics.

claim: T. brucei is a major human and animal protozoal pathogen.
source: T. brucei is also a major human and animal protozoal pathogen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. brucei's pathogenic nature.

claim: GC3 codons have a major positive impact on both mRNA and protein abundance.
source: Here, an experimental assessment, using synthetic reporter genes, revealed that GC3 codons have a major positive impact on both mRNA and protein abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using synthetic reporter genes as described in the manuscript.

claim: Estimates of relative expression based on coding sequences alone (codon usage and sequence length) are within 2-fold of the observed values for the majority of measured cellular mRNAs (n > 7000).
source: Our estimates of relative expression, based on coding sequences alone (codon usage and sequence length), are within 2-fold of the observed values for the majority of measured cellular mRNAs (n > 7000) and proteins (n > 2000).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of predicted and observed expression data from transcriptome analysis.

claim: Estimates of relative expression based on coding sequences alone (codon usage and sequence length) are within 2-fold of the observed values for the majority of measured cellular proteins (n > 2000).
source: Our estimates of relative expression, based on coding sequences alone (codon usage and sequence length), are within 2-fold of the observed values for the majority of measured cellular mRNAs (n > 7000) and proteins (n > 2000).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of predicted and observed expression data from proteome analysis.

claim: Expression estimates based on codon usage correspond with expression measures from published transcriptome and proteome datasets from other trypanosomatids.
source: Our estimates also correspond with expression measures from published transcriptome and proteome datasets from other trypanosomatids.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published datasets from other trypanosomatid species.

claim: Codon usage is a key factor affecting global relative mRNA and protein expression in trypanosomatids.
source: We conclude that codon usage is a key factor affecting global relative mRNA and protein expression in trypanosomatids and that relative abundance can be effectively estimated using only protein coding sequences.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental and bioinformatic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Relative abundance can be effectively estimated using only protein coding sequences.
source: We conclude that codon usage is a key factor affecting global relative mRNA and protein expression in trypanosomatids and that relative abundance can be effectively estimated using only protein coding sequences.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the correlation between predicted and observed expression levels.

claim: A relatively small number of 'dispersed' GT-rich RNA polymerase II (pol-II) promoters drive constitutive polycistronic transcription in T. brucei.
source: Trypanosoma brucei are parasitic protozoa that present a unique model for studies on gene expression because a relatively small number of 'dispersed' GT-rich RNA polymerase II (pol-II) promoters drive constitutive polycistronic transcription (Wedel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wedel et al., 2017.

claim: T. brucei have no known regulated RNA polymerase II promoters for protein-coding genes.
source: Indeed, T. brucei have no known regulated RNA polymerase II promoters for protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about T. brucei transcription.

claim: Some stress response genes and cell cycle regulated genes are located towards the ends of the polycistonic units.
source: Some stress response genes and cell cycle regulated genes are located towards the ends of the polycistonic units (Kelly et al., 2012) but there is otherwise limited clustering of functionally related genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2012.

claim: There is limited clustering of functionally related genes in T. brucei.
source: Some stress response genes and cell cycle regulated genes are located towards the ends of the polycistonic units (Kelly et al., 2012) but there is otherwise limited clustering of functionally related genes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about T. brucei genome organization.

claim: Trypanosomes have only two genes containing known introns.
source: In addition, trypanosomes have only two genes containing known introns (Mair et al., 2000), and every mRNA has an identical sequence trans-spliced onto the 5'-end (Clayton, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mair et al., 2000.

claim: Every mRNA in trypanosomes has an identical sequence trans-spliced onto the 5'-end.
source: In addition, trypanosomes have only two genes containing known introns (Mair et al., 2000), and every mRNA has an identical sequence trans-spliced onto the 5'-end (Clayton, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clayton, 2016.

claim: Features of transcription and mRNA processing are conserved in related parasitic trypanosomatids, Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania spp. and in other trypanosomatids.
source: These features are conserved in the related parasitic trypanosomatids, Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania spp. and in other trypanosomatids.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about trypanosomatid biology.

claim: The uniformity in transcription and mRNA processing indicates that gene expression control primarily operates post-transcription in trypanosomatids.
source: This remarkable level of uniformity in terms of transcription and mRNA processing indicates that gene expression control primarily operates post-transcription.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed uniformity in transcription and mRNA processing.

claim: Sixty-one alternative base-triplets (codons) in DNA and mRNA encode for twenty different amino acids.
source: Sixty-one alternative base-triplets (codons) in DNA and mRNA encode for twenty different amino acids, such that many amino acids are encoded by two or up to six distinct but 'synonymous' codons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic code.

claim: Many amino acids are encoded by two or up to six distinct but 'synonymous' codons.
source: Sixty-one alternative base-triplets (codons) in DNA and mRNA encode for twenty different amino acids, such that many amino acids are encoded by two or up to six distinct but 'synonymous' codons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about codon redundancy.

claim: Codons can vary in their first position for three amino acids and in their third position for eighteen.
source: These codons can vary in their first position for three amino acids and in their third position for eighteen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about codon variation.

claim: One mRNA can yield 4000 molecules of protein, as measured in yeast.
source: One mRNA can yield 4000 molecules of protein, as measured in yeast (Futcher et al., 1999), while the average protein:mRNA ratio in insect-form T. brucei is estimated to be 550:1; median values of three and 1650 molecules per gene, per cell, respectively (Kolev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Futcher et al., 1999.

claim: The average protein:mRNA ratio in insect-form T. brucei is estimated to be 550:1.
source: One mRNA can yield 4000 molecules of protein, as measured in yeast (Futcher et al., 1999), while the average protein:mRNA ratio in insect-form T. brucei is estimated to be 550:1; median values of three and 1650 molecules per gene, per cell, respectively (Kolev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kolev et al., 2010.

claim: Median values of mRNA and protein in insect-form T. brucei are three and 1650 molecules per gene, per cell, respectively.
source: One mRNA can yield 4000 molecules of protein, as measured in yeast (Futcher et al., 1999), while the average protein:mRNA ratio in insect-form T. brucei is estimated to be 550:1; median values of three and 1650 molecules per gene, per cell, respectively (Kolev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kolev et al., 2010.

claim: There is substantial capacity for expression control at the level of translation in T. brucei.
source: Thus, there is substantial capacity for expression control at the level of translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the high protein:mRNA ratio.

claim: Individual codons can control translation-rate in yeast.
source: Indeed, individual codons can control translation-rate in yeast (Gardin et al., 2014), codon-dependent local translation slowdown can facilitate nascent peptide processing in eukaryotes (Mahlab and Linial, 2014; Pechmann et al., 2014) and changes in relative codon usage and cognate tRNA abundance can control differentiation-related translation programmes in metazoa (Gingold et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gardin et al., 2014.

claim: Codon-dependent local translation slowdown can facilitate nascent peptide processing in eukaryotes.
source: Indeed, individual codons can control translation-rate in yeast (Gardin et al., 2014), codon-dependent local translation slowdown can facilitate nascent peptide processing in eukaryotes (Mahlab and Linial, 2014; Pechmann et al., 2014) and changes in relative codon usage and cognate tRNA abundance can control differentiation-related translation programmes in metazoa (Gingold et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mahlab and Linial, 2014; Pechmann et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in relative codon usage and cognate tRNA abundance can control differentiation-related translation programmes in metazoa.
source: Indeed, individual codons can control translation-rate in yeast (Gardin et al., 2014), codon-dependent local translation slowdown can facilitate nascent peptide processing in eukaryotes (Mahlab and Linial, 2014; Pechmann et al., 2014) and changes in relative codon usage and cognate tRNA abundance can control differentiation-related translation programmes in metazoa (Gingold et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gingold et al., 2014.

claim: Different codons are decoded at different rates by native ribosomes.
source: Thus, different codons are decoded at different rates by native ribosomes (Hanson and Coller, 2018; Novoa and Ribas de Pouplana, 2012; Quax et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanson and Coller, 2018; Novoa and Ribas de Pouplana, 2012; Quax et al., 2015.

claim: Codon usage can impact mRNA decay.
source: Codon usage can also impact mRNA decay (Hanson and Coller, 2018; Presnyak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanson and Coller, 2018; Presnyak et al., 2015.

claim: In trypanosomatids, highly expressed genes are amplified in tandem and are enriched in GC3 codons.
source: In trypanosomatids, highly expressed genes are amplified in tandem and are enriched in GC3 codons, those codons that have a G or a C at the third position; cognate tRNA genes for these codons also display increased copy number (Horn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horn, 2008.

claim: Cognate tRNA genes for GC3 codons display increased copy number in trypanosomatids.
source: In trypanosomatids, highly expressed genes are amplified in tandem and are enriched in GC3 codons, those codons that have a G or a C at the third position; cognate tRNA genes for these codons also display increased copy number (Horn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horn, 2008.

claim: GC3 codons are favoured in highly expressed genes in mammals.
source: Although pol-II promoters appear to underpin much of the regulation of gene expression in metazoa and other eukaryotes, GC3 codons are also favoured in highly expressed genes in mammals and the evidence suggests that protein abundance is in fact predominantly controlled at the level of translation (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwanhäusser et al., 2011.

claim: Protein abundance is predominantly controlled at the level of translation in mammals.
source: Although pol-II promoters appear to underpin much of the regulation of gene expression in metazoa and other eukaryotes, GC3 codons are also favoured in highly expressed genes in mammals and the evidence suggests that protein abundance is in fact predominantly controlled at the level of translation (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwanhäusser et al., 2011.

claim: Control of translation and mRNA stability in trypanosomatids are typically ascribed to 3'-untranslated sequences and their interactions with RNA-binding proteins.
source: In trypanosomatids, control of translation and mRNA stability are typically ascribed to 3'-untranslated sequences and their interactions with RNA-binding proteins and indeed, such regulation does operate (Clayton, 2013), but informatics analysis also supports a role for translational selection, the increased translation of GC3 codons (Chanda et al., 2007; Horn, 2008; Subramanian and Sarkar, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clayton, 2013.

claim: Informatics analysis supports a role for translational selection, the increased translation of GC3 codons in trypanosomatids.
source: In trypanosomatids, control of translation and mRNA stability are typically ascribed to 3'-untranslated sequences and their interactions with RNA-binding proteins and indeed, such regulation does operate (Clayton, 2013), but informatics analysis also supports a role for translational selection, the increased translation of GC3 codons (Chanda et al., 2007; Horn, 2008; Subramanian and Sarkar, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chanda et al., 2007; Horn, 2008; Subramanian and Sarkar, 2015.

claim: The GC3-enriched gLUC gene showed 6-fold higher luciferase expression compared to the wild-type gene as determined by densitometry.
source: We observed robust inducible expression and relative induced expression levels that were as predicted by our hypothesis, revealing 6-fold higher luciferase expression from the GC3-enriched gene as determined by densitometry (Figure 1B); three independent clones using each construct revealed similar results and we saw no evidence of toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Three independent clones using each gLUC construct revealed similar results.
source: We observed robust inducible expression and relative induced expression levels that were as predicted by our hypothesis, revealing 6-fold higher luciferase expression from the GC3-enriched gene as determined by densitometry (Figure 1B); three independent clones using each construct revealed similar results and we saw no evidence of toxicity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: There was no evidence of toxicity from gLUC expression in T. brucei.
source: We observed robust inducible expression and relative induced expression levels that were as predicted by our hypothesis, revealing 6-fold higher luciferase expression from the GC3-enriched gene as determined by densitometry (Figure 1B); three independent clones using each construct revealed similar results and we saw no evidence of toxicity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Expression from the high-GC3 gLUC gene was 4-fold higher relative to the medium-GC3 gene.
source: We observed 4-fold higher expression from the high-GC3 gene relative to the medium-GC3 gene and strikingly undetectable expression from the low-GC3 gene; in each case, a pair of independent clones derived using each construct revealed similar expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression from the low-GC3 gLUC gene was undetectable.
source: We observed 4-fold higher expression from the high-GC3 gene relative to the medium-GC3 gene and strikingly undetectable expression from the low-GC3 gene; in each case, a pair of independent clones derived using each construct revealed similar expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Codon usage has the potential to account for the full dynamic range of protein expression levels observed in trypanosomes.
source: These results indicate that codon usage has the potential to account for the full dynamic range of protein expression levels observed in trypanosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the wide range of expression levels observed with different codon usage patterns.

claim: Expression from the high-GC3 GFP gene was higher than from the medium-GC3 gene.
source: Expression from the high-GC3 GFP gene was higher than from the medium-GC3 gene and, as in the case of gLUC above, expression of the low-GC3 gene was undetectable; again, pairs of independent clones using each construct revealed similar expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of the low-GC3 GFP gene was undetectable.
source: Expression from the high-GC3 GFP gene was higher than from the medium-GC3 gene and, as in the case of gLUC above, expression of the low-GC3 gene was undetectable; again, pairs of independent clones using each construct revealed similar expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Analysis of gLUC RNA revealed increased expression from the GC3-enriched gene.
source: Analysis of gLUC RNA extracted from the T. brucei strains shown in Figure 1A revealed increased expression from the GC3-enriched gene (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mRNA expression was increased by GC3 codons.
source: These results indicated that mRNA expression was also increased by GC3 codons.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA blot analysis showing increased mRNA from GC3-enriched genes.

claim: Higher mRNA expression was observed from the high-GC3 relative to the medium-GC3 or low-GC3 gLUC and GFP genes.
source: We observed higher mRNA expression from the high-GC3 relative to the medium-GC3 or low-GC3 gLUC and GFP genes; the difference was <2 fold for gLUC but approximately 2-fold for GFP and achieved statistical significance in the latter case.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The difference in mRNA expression was <2 fold for gLUC but approximately 2-fold for GFP and achieved statistical significance in the latter case.
source: We observed higher mRNA expression from the high-GC3 relative to the medium-GC3 or low-GC3 gLUC and GFP genes; the difference was <2 fold for gLUC but approximately 2-fold for GFP and achieved statistical significance in the latter case.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Low-GC3 gLUC and GFP genes yielded slower-migrating transcripts.
source: Notably, low-GC3 gLUC and GFP genes yielded slower-migrating transcripts (Figure 2B), which may reflect longer poly(A) tails, as also observed for poorly translated mRNAs with a low proportion of optimal codons in other eukaryotes (Lima et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Slower-migrating transcripts from low-GC3 genes may reflect longer poly(A) tails, as also observed for poorly translated mRNAs with a low proportion of optimal codons in other eukaryotes.
source: Notably, low-GC3 gLUC and GFP genes yielded slower-migrating transcripts (Figure 2B), which may reflect longer poly(A) tails, as also observed for poorly translated mRNAs with a low proportion of optimal codons in other eukaryotes (Lima et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on observation and supported by citation to Lima et al., 2017.

claim: The range of differential expression for mRNA reaches almost 2-fold.
source: While the range of values reaches almost 2-fold differential for mRNA (Figure 2C), the range is substantially greater for protein (Figure 1C) pointing to an impact on translation that quantitatively exceeds the impact on mRNA levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The range of differential expression is substantially greater for protein than for mRNA, pointing to an impact on translation that quantitatively exceeds the impact on mRNA levels.
source: While the range of values reaches almost 2-fold differential for mRNA (Figure 2C), the range is substantially greater for protein (Figure 1C) pointing to an impact on translation that quantitatively exceeds the impact on mRNA levels.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of mRNA and protein expression data.

claim: The average Codon Adaptation Index (CAI) for the full set of >7,000 T. brucei genes is 0.712.
source: The average Codon Adaptation Index (CAI) (Sharp and Li, 1987) for the full set of >7,000 T. brucei genes is 0.712 (Figure 3A), with a maximal CAI of 0.883 for the α-tubulin genes.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The maximal CAI for T. brucei genes is 0.883 for the α-tubulin genes.
source: The average Codon Adaptation Index (CAI) (Sharp and Li, 1987) for the full set of >7,000 T. brucei genes is 0.712 (Figure 3A), with a maximal CAI of 0.883 for the α-tubulin genes.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The reference set of highly expressed genes has an average CAI of 0.782.
source: The reference set of highly expressed genes (see Materials and methods) has an average CAI of 0.782 (Figure 3A) and, consistent with the view that tandem amplification is another mechanism used by trypanosomatids to increase gene expression (Horn, 2008), there are many 'tandem genes' in this reference set.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There are many 'tandem genes' in the reference set of highly expressed genes.
source: The reference set of highly expressed genes (see Materials and methods) has an average CAI of 0.782 (Figure 3A) and, consistent with the view that tandem amplification is another mechanism used by trypanosomatids to increase gene expression (Horn, 2008), there are many 'tandem genes' in this reference set.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The set of genes encoding detected proteins in a published proteome dataset had a substantially higher average CAI (0.724), relative to the proteins that were not detected (0.701).
source: Importantly, the set of genes encoding detected proteins in a published proteome dataset (Urbaniak et al., 2012), had a substantially higher average CAI (0.724), relative to the proteins that were not detected (0.701, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published proteome data from Urbaniak et al., 2012.

claim: Just over 500 genes encoding abundant proteins detected in a Leishmania mexicana proteome study were enriched for high CAI values.
source: Just over 500 genes encoding abundant proteins detected in a Leishmania mexicana proteome study were also enriched for high CAI values (Paape et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published proteome data from Paape et al., 2008.

claim: Many genes immediately adjacent to divergent or convergent polycistronic transcription initiation or termination regions displayed relatively low CAI values.
source: When we assessed CAI in relation to location on trypanosomatid chromosomes; we found that many genes immediately adjacent to divergent or convergent polycistronic transcription initiation or termination regions displayed relatively low CAI values (Figure 3A,B); the full cohort of 343 of these 'strand-switch' genes yielded an average CAI of 0.685 (Figure 3A) and T. brucei chromosome 3 is shown to illustrate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The full cohort of 343 'strand-switch' genes yielded an average CAI of 0.685.
source: When we assessed CAI in relation to location on trypanosomatid chromosomes; we found that many genes immediately adjacent to divergent or convergent polycistronic transcription initiation or termination regions displayed relatively low CAI values (Figure 3A,B); the full cohort of 343 of these 'strand-switch' genes yielded an average CAI of 0.685 (Figure 3A) and T. brucei chromosome 3 is shown to illustrate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Low CAI values at strand-switch regions reflect the previous observation of base-skew asymmetry flanking these regions.
source: This reflects the previous observation of base-skew asymmetry flanking these regions (Nilsson and Andersson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nilsson and Andersson, 2005.

claim: In Leishmania major, tandem paralogous genes and genes at transcription switch regions have inflated and deflated CAI values, respectively.
source: We also assessed codon usage at the genomic scale in Leishmania major and similarly found that tandem paralogous genes and genes at transcription switch regions have inflated and deflated CAI values, respectively; L. major chromosome 1 is shown to illustrate this (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Analysis of codon representation in the reference set of highly expressed genes revealed the expected over-representation of GC3 codons, which is particularly pronounced when there are only two alternative codons for an amino acid.
source: An analysis of codon representation in the reference set of highly expressed genes revealed the expected over-representation of GC3 codons, which is particularly pronounced when there are only two alternative codons for an amino acid (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the case of xxC/T wobble codons the xxC rather than xxT version of the tRNA is always present for these amino acids (Asn, Asp, Cys, His, Phe, Tyr).
source: Indeed, in the case of xxC/T wobble codons the xxC rather than xxT version of the tRNA is always present for these amino acids (Asn, Asp, Cys, His, Phe, Tyr) (Horn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horn, 2008.

claim: When there are 3–6 alternative codons, the xxT version of the wobble tRNA is typically present (Ile, Ala, Pro, Thr, Val, Leu, Arg, SerTCT) and both alternative wobble codons are often over-represented in these cases (Ile, Ala, Leu, Arg, SerTCT).
source: In contrast, when there are 3–6 alternative codons, the xxT version of the wobble tRNA is typically present (Ile, Ala, Pro, Thr, Val, Leu, Arg, SerTCT) and both alternative wobble codons are often over-represented in these cases (Ile, Ala, Leu, Arg, SerTCT).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the codon usage analysis.

claim: Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) genes in T. brucei display unusual codon usage bias.
source: Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) genes in T. brucei, which are involved in immune evasion and are subject to allelic exclusion, display unusual codon usage bias (Alvarez et al., 1994; Chanda et al., 2007; Cross et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alvarez et al., 1994; Chanda et al., 2007; Cross et al., 2014.

claim: In VSG genes, A3 codons are over-represented, while G3 codons, and notably almost all U3 codons, are under-represented.
source: Distinct from highly expressed and indeed other gene families, A3 codons are over-represented, while G3 codons, and notably almost all U3 codons, are under-represented in the VSG genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cohort of 188 intact VSGs display low CAI values, with an average of 0.672.
source: Consistent with this, we find that the cohort of 188 intact VSGs display low CAI values (Figure 3A,B), with an average of 0.672.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The single expressed VSG produces the most abundant mRNA and protein in bloodstream form T. brucei.
source: The single expressed VSG produces the most abundant mRNA and protein in bloodstream form T. brucei but a high rate of translation is probably not required due to a high rate of transcription by RNA pol-I, combined with remarkably slow turnover of both the VSG mRNA (half-life ~4.5 hr) (Ehlers et al., 1987) and protein (half-life ~33 + /- 9 hr) (Seyfang et al., 1990); the mean mRNA half-life in bloodstream-form T. brucei is 16 min (Fadda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about VSG expression.

claim: VSG mRNA has a half-life of ~4.5 hr.
source: The single expressed VSG produces the most abundant mRNA and protein in bloodstream form T. brucei but a high rate of translation is probably not required due to a high rate of transcription by RNA pol-I, combined with remarkably slow turnover of both the VSG mRNA (half-life ~4.5 hr) (Ehlers et al., 1987) and protein (half-life ~33 + /- 9 hr) (Seyfang et al., 1990); the mean mRNA half-life in bloodstream-form T. brucei is 16 min (Fadda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ehlers et al., 1987.

claim: VSG protein has a half-life of ~33 +/- 9 hr.
source: The single expressed VSG produces the most abundant mRNA and protein in bloodstream form T. brucei but a high rate of translation is probably not required due to a high rate of transcription by RNA pol-I, combined with remarkably slow turnover of both the VSG mRNA (half-life ~4.5 hr) (Ehlers et al., 1987) and protein (half-life ~33 + /- 9 hr) (Seyfang et al., 1990); the mean mRNA half-life in bloodstream-form T. brucei is 16 min (Fadda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seyfang et al., 1990.

claim: The mean mRNA half-life in bloodstream-form T. brucei is 16 min.
source: The single expressed VSG produces the most abundant mRNA and protein in bloodstream form T. brucei but a high rate of translation is probably not required due to a high rate of transcription by RNA pol-I, combined with remarkably slow turnover of both the VSG mRNA (half-life ~4.5 hr) (Ehlers et al., 1987) and protein (half-life ~33 + /- 9 hr) (Seyfang et al., 1990); the mean mRNA half-life in bloodstream-form T. brucei is 16 min (Fadda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fadda et al., 2014.

claim: Sub-optimal translation, due to low G3 and high A3-usage in VSGs, may be necessary to prevent these multi-copy genes from compromising VSG allelic exclusion and the immune evasion strategy of bloodstream form T. brucei.
source: Indeed, sub-optimal translation, due to low G3 and high A3-usage in VSGs, may be necessary to prevent these multi-copy genes, distributed throughout the genome, from compromising VSG allelic exclusion and the immune evasion strategy of bloodstream form T. brucei.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed codon usage patterns in VSG genes.

claim: Codon-pair bias is observed in other genomes.
source: Since codon-pair bias is observed in other genomes (Quax et al., 2015), and some pair-bias combinations have the potential to be in conflict with increased codon optimality, we also examined these features of T. brucei protein-coding sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quax et al., 2015.

claim: Analysis of T. brucei protein-coding sequences revealed enrichment of duplicated codons.
source: This revealed enrichment of duplicated codons (Figure 4A) and other examples of pair-bias (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Analysis of T. brucei protein-coding sequences revealed other examples of codon pair-bias.
source: This revealed enrichment of duplicated codons (Figure 4A) and other examples of pair-bias (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Codon co-occurrence is thought to facilitate tRNA recharging.
source: Codon co-occurrence is thought to facilitate tRNA recharging, while the over-represented (examples include xxC/Axx, xxU/Gxx, xxC/xxC and xxG/xxG) and under-represented (examples include xxA/Gxx, xxU/Axx, xxC/xxG, xxG/xxC) pairs (Figure 4B,C) are thought to reflect more optimal tRNA interactions at the A and P sites that impact translation fidelity (Quax et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about codon pair bias, supported by citation to Quax et al., 2015.

claim: Over-represented codon pairs (examples include xxC/Axx, xxU/Gxx, xxC/xxC and xxG/xxG) and under-represented pairs (examples include xxA/Gxx, xxU/Axx, xxC/xxG, xxG/xxC) are thought to reflect more optimal tRNA interactions at the A and P sites that impact translation fidelity.
source: Codon co-occurrence is thought to facilitate tRNA recharging, while the over-represented (examples include xxC/Axx, xxU/Gxx, xxC/xxC and xxG/xxG) and under-represented (examples include xxA/Gxx, xxU/Axx, xxC/xxG, xxG/xxC) pairs (Figure 4B,C) are thought to reflect more optimal tRNA interactions at the A and P sites that impact translation fidelity (Quax et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about codon pair bias, supported by citation to Quax et al., 2015.

claim: An over-representation of xxU/Gxx pairs, and under-representation of xxC/xxG and xxG/xxC pairs, limits the accumulation of 'optimal' GC3 codons.
source: We do note, however, that an over-representation of xxU/Gxx pairs, and under-representation of xxC/xxG and xxG/xxC pairs, limits the accumulation of 'optimal' GC3 codons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the codon pair bias analysis.

claim: The new T. brucei transcriptome dataset comprised three replicates with >114 million mapped reads and yielded pair-wise Pearson correlation coefficients of >0.999.
source: This dataset comprised three replicates, was of sufficient depth to provide >114 million mapped reads, and yielded pair-wise Pearson correlation coefficients of >0.999 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: An initial comparison of mRNA and peptide expression yielded a Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.57.
source: An initial comparison of mRNA and peptide expression yielded a Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.57 (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: mRNA abundance is predictive of protein abundance in T. brucei.
source: Thus, as in other cell types (Ly et al., 2014), mRNA abundance is predictive of protein abundance.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between mRNA and protein expression, and supported by citation to Ly et al., 2014.

claim: The relationship between mRNA and protein abundance displays the best fit with a logarithmic trend-line.
source: This relationship displays the best fit with a logarithmic trend-line, whereas the best fit is with a linear trend-line when only 10% of the most highly expressed mRNAs are excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The best fit is with a linear trend-line when only 10% of the most highly expressed mRNAs are excluded from the analysis of mRNA-protein relationship.
source: This relationship displays the best fit with a logarithmic trend-line, whereas the best fit is with a linear trend-line when only 10% of the most highly expressed mRNAs are excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The logarithmic relationship between mRNA and protein may reflect poor translation of highly abundant mRNA's, as noted previously for transcripts encoding ribosomal proteins.
source: This may reflect poor translation of highly abundant mRNA's, as noted previously for transcripts encoding ribosomal proteins (Antwi et al., 2016), but might equally reflect experimental bias due to limitations in the effective dynamic range of proteome analysis (Urbaniak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Antwi et al., 2016.

claim: The logarithmic relationship between mRNA and protein might reflect experimental bias due to limitations in the effective dynamic range of proteome analysis.
source: This may reflect poor translation of highly abundant mRNA's, as noted previously for transcripts encoding ribosomal proteins (Antwi et al., 2016), but might equally reflect experimental bias due to limitations in the effective dynamic range of proteome analysis (Urbaniak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Urbaniak et al., 2012.

claim: Short genes produce relatively more mRNA in T. brucei.
source: Short genes produce relatively more mRNA in T. brucei (Fadda et al., 2014; Jha et al., 2014), so we also considered gene length for our analysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fadda et al., 2014; Jha et al., 2014.

claim: Gene length is inversely correlated with mRNA expression.
source: Indeed, we found that gene length is inversely correlated with both mRNA expression in our dataset (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2) and with protein expression (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2) and that long genes tend to make less mRNA and protein.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Gene length is inversely correlated with protein expression.
source: Indeed, we found that gene length is inversely correlated with both mRNA expression in our dataset (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2) and with protein expression (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2) and that long genes tend to make less mRNA and protein.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Long genes tend to make less mRNA and protein.
source: Indeed, we found that gene length is inversely correlated with both mRNA expression in our dataset (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2) and with protein expression (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2) and that long genes tend to make less mRNA and protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverse correlation between gene length and expression.

claim: Analysis of the correspondence between codon usage and observed T. brucei mRNA expression (n = 7225) yielded a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.48.
source: An analysis of the correspondence between codon usage and observed T. brucei mRNA expression (n = 7225) yielded a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.48 (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A measure of mRNA abundance can be predicted based on the coding-sequence alone.
source: We found this quite remarkable, that a measure of mRNA abundance can be predicted based on the coding-sequence alone.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: A penalty for coding-sequence length [CAI - (0.03 x √coding sequence length in kbp)] improved the correspondence between CAI-values and observed mRNA expression and yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.52.
source: Since shorter coding-sequences yield more mRNA (Figure 5B), we derived a simple formula including a penalty for coding-sequence length [CAI - (0.03 x √coding sequence length in kbp)]. This penalty improved the correspondence between CAI-values and observed mRNA expression and yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.52 (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2); using this approach,>70% of our estimates of relative expression are within 2-fold of the observed values (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Using the length-adjusted CAI approach, >70% of estimates of relative mRNA expression are within 2-fold of the observed values.
source: Since shorter coding-sequences yield more mRNA (Figure 5B), we derived a simple formula including a penalty for coding-sequence length [CAI - (0.03 x √coding sequence length in kbp)]. This penalty improved the correspondence between CAI-values and observed mRNA expression and yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.52 (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2); using this approach,>70% of our estimates of relative expression are within 2-fold of the observed values (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Analysis of codon usage in relation to protein expression (n = 2315) revealed a correlation coefficient of 0.55.
source: A similar analysis of the impact of codon usage on the proteome of T. brucei (n = 2315) also revealed a substantially improved correlation when we applied the same penalty for coding-sequence length. In this case, the correlation between CAI values and observed protein expression yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.55 (Figure 6D, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2), which increased to 0.65 following the length-adjustment (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2); again,>70% of our estimates of relative expression are within 2-fold of the observed values (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The correlation between CAI values and observed protein expression increased to 0.65 following the length-adjustment.
source: A similar analysis of the impact of codon usage on the proteome of T. brucei (n = 2315) also revealed a substantially improved correlation when we applied the same penalty for coding-sequence length. In this case, the correlation between CAI values and observed protein expression yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.55 (Figure 6D, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2), which increased to 0.65 following the length-adjustment (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2); again,>70% of our estimates of relative expression are within 2-fold of the observed values (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Using the length-adjusted CAI approach, >70% of estimates of relative protein expression are within 2-fold of the observed values.
source: A similar analysis of the impact of codon usage on the proteome of T. brucei (n = 2315) also revealed a substantially improved correlation when we applied the same penalty for coding-sequence length. In this case, the correlation between CAI values and observed protein expression yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.55 (Figure 6D, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2), which increased to 0.65 following the length-adjustment (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 1, sheet 2); again,>70% of our estimates of relative expression are within 2-fold of the observed values (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq data from bloodstream-form T. brucei revealed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and RNA-seq expression data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.54.
source: Using these data, minus those 2.8% of genes that differed >3 fold between stages (201 of 7191 genes), we once again observed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and RNA-seq expression data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B). Pearson correlation coefficients were 0.54 and 0.53 for the bloodstream-form (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and insect-form data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), respectively (improved by 5.5% and 4.6% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq data from insect-form T. brucei revealed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and RNA-seq expression data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.53.
source: Using these data, minus those 2.8% of genes that differed >3 fold between stages (201 of 7191 genes), we once again observed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and RNA-seq expression data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B). Pearson correlation coefficients were 0.54 and 0.53 for the bloodstream-form (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and insect-form data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), respectively (improved by 5.5% and 4.6% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNA-seq data from insect-form cells generated by another research group also revealed correspondence with length-adjusted CAI values with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.5.
source: RNA-seq data from insect-form cells generated by another research group (Christiano et al., 2017) also revealed correspondence with length-adjusted CAI values (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). The Pearson correlation coefficient was 0.5 in this case (improved by 3% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and citation to Christiano et al., 2017.

claim: The findings on codon usage and expression apply to multiple T. brucei life cycle stages and to independently generated datasets.
source: Thus, our findings apply to multiple T. brucei life cycle stages and to independently generated datasets.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of multiple datasets from different life cycle stages and research groups.

claim: For cohorts of genes encoding components of protein complexes or related functions (n = 23), codon usage-based predictions, when compared to observed measures, yielded a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.84.
source: For these cohorts (n = 23), codon usage-based predictions, when compared to observed measures, yielded a striking Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.84 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The strong correlation between predicted and observed expression for protein cohorts reinforces the view that codon usage bias plays a major role in controlling protein expression.
source: This further reinforces the view that codon usage bias plays a major role in controlling protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation coefficient for protein cohorts.

claim: Relative expression estimates were derived based on 19,000 non-VSG mRNAs and 100 million non-VSG proteins per bloodstream form cell.
source: Using our relative expression estimates, we derived values for numbers of both mRNA and protein molecules per bloodstream form cell (Supplementary File 1, sheet 2). These are based on 19,000 non-VSG mRNAs (Haanstra et al., 2008) and 100 million non-VSG proteins per cell, similar to estimates for yeast (Milo, 2013).
evidence: This is based on published estimates from Haanstra et al., 2008 and Milo, 2013.

claim: The abundance of the cell cycle specific kinetochore complex is 3.7-fold below the predictions based on the trend-line.
source: Indeed, we see examples of such complexes in Figure 7; the abundance of the cell cycle specific kinetochore complex (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014) and the bloodstream down-regulated editosome complex (Stuart et al., 2005) are 3.7-fold and 2.7-fold below the predictions based on the trend-line, respectively (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7 and citation to Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014.

claim: The abundance of the bloodstream down-regulated editosome complex is 2.7-fold below the predictions based on the trend-line.
source: Indeed, we see examples of such complexes in Figure 7; the abundance of the cell cycle specific kinetochore complex (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014) and the bloodstream down-regulated editosome complex (Stuart et al., 2005) are 3.7-fold and 2.7-fold below the predictions based on the trend-line, respectively (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7 and citation to Stuart et al., 2005.

claim: The abundance of the o-sector of the V-ATPase is 2.5-fold below the prediction, reflecting under-representation of membrane–associated proteins in peptide-based proteomic strategies.
source: Notably, the analyses shown in Figure 7 also appears to reflect a particular technical limitation typically seen when using peptide-based proteomic strategies, the under-representation of membrane–associated proteins; the abundance of the o-sector of the V-ATPase (Baker et al., 2015) is 2.5-fold below the prediction on this plot.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7 and citation to Baker et al., 2015.

claim: A comparison between predicted expression values and published ribosome profiling data revealed correspondence with measures of translation efficiency with a correlation coefficient of 0.35.
source: To explore this possibility, we compared our predicted expression values with published ribosome profiling data (Vasquez et al., 2014) and observed correspondence with measures of translation efficiency (Figure 8A); the correlation coefficient was 0.35 (improved by 6.8% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8A and citation to Vasquez et al., 2014.

claim: A comparison between CAI values and published T. brucei mRNA half-life data revealed a correspondence with a correlation coefficient of 0.37.
source: Indeed, a comparison between CAI values and published T. brucei mRNA half-life data (Fadda et al., 2014) revealed a correspondence (Figure 8B); the correlation coefficient was 0.37.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8B and citation to Fadda et al., 2014.

claim: Correspondence between CAI and mRNA half-life decreased when the length-adjustment was applied, supporting the view that codon usage bias controls mRNA stability in a length-independent manner.
source: Notably, correspondence decreased (3.2% in bloodstream-form cells; or improved only 0.3% in insect-stage cells) when the length-adjustment was applied in this case. This supports the view that codon usage bias controls mRNA stability in a length-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the relationship between CAI and mRNA half-life.

claim: Optimal codons increase ribosome occupancy and translation, which in turn protects mRNA from decapping/deadenylation, thereby also increasing mRNA stability.
source: We suggest that optimal codons increase ribosome occupancy and translation, which in turn protects mRNA from (length-independent) decapping/deadenylation, thereby also increasing mRNA stability.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed correlations.

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq data from Trypanosoma vivax revealed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and RNA-seq expression data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.47.
source: We, therefore, analysed previously published RNA-seq and proteomic data from Trypanosoma vivax, another African trypanosome that causes disease in cattle and other livestock (Jackson et al., 2015). Using these data, we observed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and both RNA-seq (Figure 9A) and proteomic (Figure 9B) expression data. The Pearson correlation coefficients were 0.47 and 0.63, respectively (improved by 2.1% and 10% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9A and citation to Jackson et al., 2015.

claim: Analysis of proteomic data from Trypanosoma vivax revealed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and proteomic expression data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.63.
source: We, therefore, analysed previously published RNA-seq and proteomic data from Trypanosoma vivax, another African trypanosome that causes disease in cattle and other livestock (Jackson et al., 2015). Using these data, we observed correspondence between length-adjusted CAI values and both RNA-seq (Figure 9A) and proteomic (Figure 9B) expression data. The Pearson correlation coefficients were 0.47 and 0.63, respectively (improved by 2.1% and 10% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9B and citation to Jackson et al., 2015.

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq data from Leishmania mexicana revealed correspondence with length-adjusted CAI values with a correlation coefficient of 0.43.
source: This was also the case (Figure 9C) when we analysed RNA-seq data from Leishmania mexicana (Fiebig et al., 2015), a trypanosomatid parasite thought to have diverged from the African trypanosome lineage >120 million years ago (Harkins et al., 2016); the correlation coefficient was 0.43 (improved by 2.4% by the length-adjustment).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 9C and citations to Fiebig et al., 2015 and Harkins et al., 2016.

claim: Codon usage bias and gene length control mRNA and protein expression in many, if not all, trypanosomatids.
source: These findings support the view that codon usage bias, and gene length, control mRNA and protein expression in many, if not all, trypanosomatids.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of multiple trypanosomatid species.

claim: Relative expression can be predicted for the full complement of proteins, including thousands of proteins that fail to register in current proteome datasets.
source: Indeed, relative expression can now be predicted for the full complement of proteins, including thousands of proteins that fail to register in current proteome datasets (Supplementary file 1, sheet 2).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the predictive models developed.

claim: Codon usage contributes to gene expression control but it can be challenging to investigate the impact of codon usage bias at a genomic and proteomic scale in most eukaryotes because gene expression control operates at many levels, through transcription control in particular.
source: Codon usage contributes to gene expression control but it can be challenging to investigate the impact of codon usage bias at a genomic and proteomic scale in most eukaryotes because gene expression control operates at many levels, through transcription control in particular.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the challenges in studying codon usage.

claim: Trypanosomatids display constitutive RNA pol-II transcription and rely heavily upon post-transcriptional control, consequently presenting excellent models for the study of mRNA stability and translation control.
source: Trypanosomatids display constitutive RNA pol-II transcription and, therefore, rely heavily upon post-transcriptional control, consequently presenting excellent models for the study of mRNA stability and translation control.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about trypanosomatid biology.

claim: Codon usage has a major impact on gene expression in T. brucei.
source: We now show that codon usage has a major impact on gene expression in T. brucei and that both relative mRNA and protein expression can be predicted based on coding sequence alone.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and bioinformatic analyses.

claim: Both relative mRNA and protein expression can be predicted based on coding sequence alone in T. brucei.
source: We now show that codon usage has a major impact on gene expression in T. brucei and that both relative mRNA and protein expression can be predicted based on coding sequence alone.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental and bioinformatic analyses.

claim: Codon optimality increases mRNA stability in yeast by reducing Dhh1p-dependent decay.
source: Although to a lesser extent, mRNA abundance was also dependent upon codon usage. Indeed, codon optimality increases mRNA stability in yeast (Presnyak et al., 2015), by reducing Dhh1p-dependent decay (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Presnyak et al., 2015 and Radhakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: Under-sampling is one of the major current challenges in terms of determining relative protein abundance in cells and tissues.
source: Under-sampling is one of the major current challenges in terms of determining relative protein abundance in cells and tissues (Ly et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ly et al., 2014.

claim: For proteins that form multi-component complexes, protein turnover is likely dependent upon complex assembly, with destabilisation of unassembled subunits.
source: Notably, for proteins that form multi-component complexes, protein turnover is likely dependent upon complex assembly, with destabilisation of unassembled subunits.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about protein complex assembly and turnover.

claim: Gene length has an impact on mRNA and protein expression, proposed to be due to increased turnover of longer transcripts.
source: In addition to codon usage, gene length also has an impact on mRNA and protein expression, and this is proposed to be due to increased turnover of longer transcripts (Fadda et al., 2014; Jha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fadda et al., 2014; Jha et al., 2014.

claim: Transcript length may have a greater impact on co-transcriptional degradation rather than on co-translational degradation.
source: When we applied a gene-length adjustment, this failed to improve the correspondence between codon usage and mRNA half-life, consistent with the idea suggested previously (Fadda et al., 2014) that transcript length has a greater impact on co-transcriptional degradation rather than on co-translational degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis and supported by citation to Fadda et al., 2014.

claim: Co-transcriptional degradation may be dominated by length-dependent endonuclease activity while co-translational degradation may be dominated by length-independent exonuclease activity, following decapping and deadenylation.
source: Perhaps the former is dominated by (length-dependent) endonuclease activity while the latter is dominated by (length-independent) exonuclease activity, following decapping and deadenylation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms of mRNA degradation.

claim: Possible crosstalk between translation and mRNA decay in T. brucei was noted previously.
source: Indeed, possible crosstalk between translation and mRNA decay in T. brucei was noted previously (Antwi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Antwi et al., 2016.

claim: Optimal-codons reduce mRNA turnover in trypanosomes by increasing the rate of translation, increasing the association with actively translating ribosomes, and thereby protecting mRNA from degradation.
source: We propose that optimal-codons reduce mRNA turnover in trypanosomes by increasing the rate of translation, increasing the association with actively translating ribosomes, and thereby protecting mRNA from degradation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed correlations.

claim: Slow translation or stalling would promote mRNA degradation.
source: In this scenario, slow translation or stalling would promote mRNA degradation (Deana and Belasco, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deana and Belasco, 2005.

claim: mRNA decay is known to be co-translational in yeast.
source: Indeed, mRNA decay is known to be co-translational in yeast (Hu et al., 2009; Pelechano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2009; Pelechano et al., 2015.

claim: Estimates for highly expressed genes in yeast yield initiation rates of once every two seconds and elongation rates up to twenty amino acids per second.
source: For reference, estimates for highly expressed genes in yeast yield initiation rates of once every two seconds and elongation rates up to twenty amino acids per second (Futcher et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Futcher et al., 1999.

claim: It is estimated that there are 125,000 ribosomes and 19,000 non-VSG mRNA molecules per bloodstream form T. brucei cell.
source: In T. brucei, it is estimated that there are 125,000 ribosomes and 19,000 non-VSG mRNA molecules per bloodstream form cell (Haanstra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haanstra et al., 2008.

claim: A number of studies point to translation initiation as the rate-limiting step in protein synthesis.
source: Notably, a number of studies point to translation initiation as the rate-limiting step in protein synthesis (Jackson et al., 2010) and ribosome occupancy was found to be similar on optimised and non-optimised constructs in yeast (Presnyak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jackson et al., 2010 and Presnyak et al., 2015.

claim: Ribosome occupancy was found to be similar on optimised and non-optimised constructs in yeast.
source: Notably, a number of studies point to translation initiation as the rate-limiting step in protein synthesis (Jackson et al., 2010) and ribosome occupancy was found to be similar on optimised and non-optimised constructs in yeast (Presnyak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Presnyak et al., 2015.

claim: A constant translation initiation rate combined with variable elongation rates would be expected to yield rapidly translated mRNAs loaded with relatively few ribosomes and slowly translated mRNAs loaded with many, potentially stalled, ribosomes.
source: In simple terms, a constant translation initiation rate combined with variable elongation rates would be expected to yield rapidly translated mRNAs loaded with relatively few ribosomes and slowly translated mRNAs loaded with many, potentially stalled, ribosomes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between initiation, elongation, and ribosome occupancy.

claim: The analysis indicates correspondence between optimal codons and ribosome occupancy in trypanosomes.
source: In contrast to this scenario, however, our analysis indicates correspondence between optimal codons and ribosome occupancy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: Correspondence between optimal codons and ribosome occupancy suggests a coupling between elongation and initiation in trypanosomes which could be explained by slow ribosomes affecting trailing ribosomes and decreasing the initiation rate.
source: This suggests a coupling between elongation and initiation in trypanosomes which could be explained by slow ribosomes affecting trailing ribosomes and decreasing the initiation rate (Chu et al., 2014; Hanson and Coller, 2018) or by ribosome recycling on the same mRNA [see Supplementary information S5 in (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Chu et al., 2014; Hanson and Coller, 2018; Jackson et al., 2010.

claim: Correspondence between optimal codons and ribosome occupancy could be explained by ribosome recycling on the same mRNA.
source: This suggests a coupling between elongation and initiation in trypanosomes which could be explained by slow ribosomes affecting trailing ribosomes and decreasing the initiation rate (Chu et al., 2014; Hanson and Coller, 2018) or by ribosome recycling on the same mRNA [see Supplementary information S5 in (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Jackson et al., 2010.

claim: Protein-coding sequence composition contributes to differences in steady-state mRNA and protein abundance in trypanosomatids.
source: We conclude that protein-coding sequence composition contributes to differences in steady-state mRNA and protein abundance in trypanosomatids.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The ability to predict relative expression based on protein-coding sequences alone indicates that codon usage makes a major contribution to the transcriptomes and proteomes of trypanosomatid cells.
source: The ability to predict relative expression, based on protein-coding sequences alone, indicates that codon usage makes a major contribution to the transcriptomes and proteomes of these cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The results support a model whereby translation rate is increased by optimal codons, resulting in reduced mRNA turnover.
source: Our results support a model whereby translation rate is increased by optimal codons, resulting in reduced mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.
